checkpoints: When an `ioredis` `Cluster` client is constructed without a `scaleReads` option, the default `scaleReads: 'master'` sends every command — reads and writes alike — to the master that owns the key's hash slot, so the replicas never receive any read traffic at all.

Setting `scaleReads: 'slave'` (or `'all'`) makes ioredis issue `READONLY` on replica connections and route read-only commands such as `GET` to a replica, spreading a read-heavy workload like `product:${id}` lookups across otherwise idle replicas instead of piling it all onto the masters.

Replication from a Redis master to its replicas is asynchronous, so a value read from a replica can lag the master by some amount of time; only reads that can tolerate that staleness should be routed to replicas, while any operation that must observe its own very-recent write needs to stay pinned to the master.

Redis replicas exist primarily for availability and failover — when a master fails, one of its replicas is promoted to take over that slot range — but a replica does not accept writes and does not own any hash slots of its own.

Adding more replicas to masters that are already saturated does nothing to relieve that saturation unless the read routing is also changed, because an idle replica stays idle for reads until the client is explicitly configured to send read commands there.
Growing a Redis Cluster's actual write and keyspace capacity requires adding more masters and resharding hash slots onto them, not increasing the number of replicas attached to the existing masters.

"Availability" (surviving a master failure through promotion) and "capacity" (how much read/write throughput the cluster can absorb) are two distinct properties of a Redis Cluster, so a plan that only adds replicas improves the former without touching the latter.

A read-routing change like this should be validated with an actual load-test measurement — comparing read throughput/latency with reads sent to replicas versus everything pinned to masters — and by confirming write throughput is unchanged and still bounded solely by the number of masters, rather than trusting a code review alone.
